catalog_quote: 4.2.2.5 Lexical accent in Hittite. It was shown in the preceding sections that every prosodic word in Hittite had a single most prosodically prominent syllable, the bearer of primary stress (CULMINATIVE + OBLIGATORY; cf. §4.2.2.1). Any syllable of a word could bear stress (UNBOUNDED; cf. §4.2.2.3), but within the word, its position was phonologically unpredictable and contrastive (FREE; cf. §4.2.2.2). A word's surface stress pattern depends instead on its morphological constituency, and more specifically, stress falls preferentially on accented morphemes (MORPHOLOGY-DEPENDENT + ACCENT-CONDITIONED; cf. §4.2.2.4). With these properties established, it is now clear that Hittite has an LA system ... [§4.2.2.2] All Hittite words were stressed, but within the word the position of stress was FREE. sweep_summary: Hittite (hitt1242) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Yates 2017. this search of works with stress in the title's only title-keyword item is that same dissertation (already listed). Re-downloaded the author copy today (eScholarship could not be reached by automated download;2.2.2 (p.110) and §4.2.2.5 (p.115): every word has one primary stress, position free and unbounded, set by lexically accented morphemes with a leftmost default, no secondary stress. The catalog quote is verbatim; coding confirmed, nothing supersedes it. Held supporting papers (Yates 2015, 2016 PLSA, 2021 slides) read and agree; the 2021 slides carry Kloekhorst 2014:643 verbatim ('a stress accent that was free.. the place of the accent is lexically determined'). Only acquisition target: Kloekhorst 2014 Accent in Hittite (StBoT 56, print only), priority high as the one authoritative treatment not yet obtained first-hand.

No secondary stress evidenced (p.110). This is the catalog's existing deciding source, re-downloaded and verified verbatim today; the catalog's classification 'lexical' stands.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote check: both deciding passages (Yates 2017 p.115 §4.2.2.5 and p.110 §4.2.2.2 with ex.153) and the supporting Kloekhorst 2008 p.32 sentence are verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated locators. The deciding source is a 2017 dissertation devoted to Hittite lexical accent, open access and held in full; for an extinct language known from cuneiform this (together with Kloekhorst 2014) is the ceiling of available description. The one major unheld work, Kloekhorst 2014 StBoT 56, states the same conclusion (free, lexically determined, no positional restriction; p.643 as quoted in Yates 2021 slides downloaded now), and two further Yates papers downloaded now (PLSA 2016, WeCIEC 27) restate culminative/free/unbounded/lexical-accent. No database (StressTyp2/WALS) entry exists to contradict. Coding lexical, domain word, no secondary stress -- all supported; no reclassification or re-read needed.

sources.citation: Yates, Anthony D. 2021. Hittite and the Indo-European Accent: A conversation with Alwin Kloekhorst. Invited lecture slides, University of Oxford, 2 Dec 2021 (163 pp).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Quotes Kloekhorst (2014:643): 'Hittite had a stress accent that was free: although for each word the place of the accent is lexically determined, there is in principle no restriction as to which syllable in a given word can or cannot be accented.' Yates adds: '(i) FREE -- i.e., phonologically unpredictable, dependent on lexically specific morphological factors -- in both nominals and verbs. (ii) UNBOUNDED -- i.e., potentially surfaces on any syllable within the word (viz., no window restrictions).'
sources.note: Both authorities (Yates, Kloekhorst) agree: free, lexically determined, unbounded stress accent; slides carry the only verbatim text of Kloekhorst 2014's conclusion that we hold.

sources.quote: 'CULMINATIVITY ... each Hittite word had a single most prosodically prominent syllable (i.e. stressed), whose vowel is optionally written plene. ... Another feature common to these languages is FREE STRESS. In Hittite, stress can occur on any syllable of a prosodic word, with no evident phonological restrictions (e.g. an edge-oriented window) on its surface distribution. ... Hittite stress cannot be predicted on the basis of purely phonological factors such as metrical structure or syllable weight; rather ... morphological constituency is the primary determinant of word stress. sources.note: Same author, shorter published statement: culminative, free (any syllable, no window), morphology-driven lexical accent; BAP (leftmost accented morpheme, else leftmost syllable).

sources.citation: Yates, Anthony D. 2015. Anatolian Default Accentuation and its Diachronic Consequences. Indo-European Linguistics 3: 145-187.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Argues for default leftmost stress in words lacking an accented morpheme (the BAP default already recorded in the secondary rule); consistent with a lexical-accent system.
sources.note: Argues for a leftmost default within a lexical-accent system ('default accentuation, which applies when no constituent morpheme in a prosodic word is lexically specified as accented and assigns an earlier reading to its leftmost syllable'); refines the catalog's secondary rule, does not change the lexical coding.

sources.quote: Kloekhorst (2014:643) concludes (cf. Melchert 1994:47, 187, i.a.): "Hittite had a stress accent that was free: although for each word the place of the accent is lexically determined, there is in principle no restriction as to which syllable in a given word can or cannot be accented. . . [T]he place of the accent in a Hittite word often can be directly equated with the place of the accent in the corresponding word in Greek or Vedic Sanskrit."
sources.locator: p.643 (conclusion), as quoted in Yates 2021 slides, 'Q1: Hittite as a source for accentual reconstruction'
sources.note: The only book-length philological study of Hittite accent; its conclusion (p.643) is known to us only second-hand via Yates 2021 slides -- holding it would let the record cite both authoritative treatments directly and check Kloekhorst's clitic/function-word claims.
